text:
Welcome to CLUE!

CLUE is a platform that helps your class figure things out together as a community of scientists and engineers. On clue you can work individually and in a group, and you can share your ideas with the class and see other people's ideas.

In CLUE, everyone works in a group. When you start an activity, you can choose a group. You can change groups by clicking on the group number in the upper right corner. Then, you can either join an existing group or start a new group.

Right now, make sure you are in the same group as the other students you are sitting and working with. If your groupmates need help, help them! You're figuring things out together.

tiles.title: Lesson Structure in the Lessons and Resources Pane

text:
Each lesson in CLUE has four parts. The orange tabs above show each part.

You're engineering a new device, and the parts can help you organize your thinking.

  • Investigate: This is where you'll start thinking about a new problem and figuring out the science behind it.
  • Design: This is where you'll start designing a solution to that problem. It might be a small improvement, but that's how engineers do it -- piece by piece!
  • Develop: This is where you'll actually develop your solution -- sometimes you'll work with hardware, sometimes with software, and sometimes you'll develop your ideas in other ways.
  • Evaluate: Science and engineering aren't about figuring everything out all at once, it's about making incremental progress. After you develop something, you'll spend some time evaluating it: What worked? What didn't? Why? What are your next steps?

When you're done with one part, go to the next one.

tiles.title: How to pick up a CLUE tile

objects.text: When you hover your mouse over any tile in CLUE, a little triangle will appear that will let you pick up the tile and move it to your work space.

text:
Okay, you know the basics! Let's jump into figuring things out!

Biological hands can do a LOT of things! Plus, your brain and muscles are already "wired" to work well with a hand.

Even though we might not make something that looks or works exactly the same, understanding how hands work can give us good ideas about how to design prostheses.

tiles.title: How many different ways can you move an object?

text:
Work with your group ...

What motion are you making with your hand when you move the object?
Researchers from the University of Southern California and MIT used images from medical scans to make simulations of the hand.

Passive:

1) What do you know about bionic arms? (e.g., what they look like, why people might use them, in what ways are they connected to the person’s body, how they work)

2) If you were tasked to design a bionic arm, what do you think the people who use them would like in terms of appearance and function?
